To get involved, you can click on the links in the comments below to expand the conversation and add your thoughts. We'll continue to highlight more comments worth visiting as the day goes on. What's the best thing about dining on your own? The people-watching In this month's food column, Jay Rayner wrote that: "The pleasures of eating alone, obvious. You get to eat what you want, how you want. It is one of adulthood's great indulgences. But who admits to its other profound pleasure, the licence it gives you to spy on people?" You responded with some of your own experiences. 'I've met some interesting people that way' 'Good eating for me is inextricably linked with good company' 'I take a good book and do some people-watching' What being a care worker taught me: the human spirit needs more than the basics Community care worker, Sarah Beauclerk wrote about her moving experiences as a care worker which prompted readers to talk about what they learned looking after others. 'This job taught me some things about our society that I strongly criticise and hate' 'Daily living aids and assistive technology can help people continue to live their lives with dignity' Why the nights are getting brighter - but not in a good way Many of you who like to look up at the stars were concerned to hear satellite observations show light pollution is spreading and affecting the level of darkness across the world. ------- Please generate a story based on the sentences provided. Include keywords ['date', 'nose', 'significance', 'stomach', 'writing'] in the response.

Sarah closed her laptop after reading the Guardian article, her stomach rumbling as she glanced at the clock. It was well past her usual dinner date with herself at the corner bistro. As a care worker who spent her days tending to others, these solo meals had taken on special significance in her life.

She grabbed her notebook – the one reserved for writing observations – and headed out into the evening. The light pollution mentioned in the article was evident even here, the stars barely visible above the city's glow.

At the restaurant, she settled into her favorite corner table, pressing her nose against the cool window glass for a moment before ordering. The waiter, recognizing her as a regular, didn't question her solitary presence anymore.

As she waited for her meal, Sarah opened her notebook and began writing about the elderly gentleman at the next table who was carefully cutting his food into precise squares. She'd learned from her work that such rituals often held deep significance for people, small acts of control in an increasingly chaotic world.

Her phone buzzed with a message from a colleague asking if she wanted to join a group for drinks, but Sarah politely declined. Tonight, like many nights, she needed this time alone – to observe, to digest not just her food but the weight of caring for others day after day.

When her pasta arrived, she ate slowly, savoring each bite while continuing her writing. Through the window, despite the light pollution, she could make out Venus hanging bright and solitary in the sky, a kindred spirit in the vast urban landscape.
